title: Elements, monomers and condensation/hydrolysis; Monosaccharides and disaccharides
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: BM02#t1 term and clue written for the game; BM03#t1 term and clue written for the game; BM02#t2 term and clue written for the game; BM02#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: BM02#N.8a, BM03#N.3, BM02#N.10a, BM03#N.7a, BM03#N.10a.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Monomer
items.clue: A small unit from which larger molecules are made

items.label: Monosaccharide
items.clue: A single sugar unit: the building block of carbohydrates

items.label: Polymer
items.clue: A large molecule made of many small units joined together

items.label: Condensation
items.clue: Joining reaction that releases one water molecule for each bond formed

questions.stem: Two monosaccharides are joined by a condensation reaction to form a disaccharide. What happens in this reaction?

options.text: A molecule of water is taken in and split to supply the atoms that join the monomers
A covalent bond forms between the monomers and a molecule of water is released
A hydrogen bond forms between the two monomers, holding them together as a disaccharide
Water dissolves the two monomers so that they meet, but no water is formed or used

questions.explanation: An –OH from one monomer and an –H from the other combine to form water, leaving a covalent (glycosidic) bond between the monomers.

questions.stem: Two monosaccharides, P and Q, are drawn in their ring forms. In P the ring is made of four carbon atoms and one oxygen atom, with one further carbon atom (in a CH₂OH group) attached outside the ring. In Q the ring is also made of four carbon atoms and one oxygen atom, but two further carbon atoms (each in a CH₂OH group) are attached outside the ring. How should P and Q be classified?

options.text: Both P and Q are pentose sugars
Both P and Q are hexose sugars
P is a pentose and Q is a hexose
P and Q are alpha and beta glucose

questions.stem: A polypeptide made of 100 amino acids is completely hydrolysed into free amino acids. How many water molecules are used in the process?

options.text: 99 water molecules
100 water molecules
1 water molecule
0 water molecules

questions.explanation: 100 amino acids are joined by 99 peptide bonds. Each hydrolysis breaks one bond and uses one water molecule, split to supply the –H and –OH.

questions.stem: The enzyme maltase, in the small intestine, acts on maltose. Which statement describes the reaction?

options.text: Condensation: a glycosidic bond forms and a water molecule is released.
Hydrolysis: a hydrogen bond between two glucose molecules is broken.
Hydrolysis: a glycosidic bond is broken, using water, giving two glucose.
Hydrolysis: a glycosidic bond is broken, releasing water, giving two glucose.

questions.explanation: Maltose is glucose + glucose. One water is split; –H and –OH go to the two products.

questions.stem: Galactose and glucose both have the formula C₆H₁₂O₆ and both form a ring of five carbons and one oxygen. They differ only in which way the –OH on carbon 4 points. Which statement is correct?

options.text: They are isomers: two hexoses with the same atoms arranged differently.
They must have different formulae, because they are different sugars.
They are α-glucose and β-glucose, the same sugar drawn in two different ways.
Galactose is a pentose, as only five carbons are in its ring.

questions.explanation: Same formula, different arrangement. Like glucose and fructose in the hook, that is enough to make a different sugar with a different shape.
